title: Stay safe in an earthquake, storm, fire, flood or tsunami
short: Earthquake, tsunami, hurricane, tornado, thunderstorm, wildfire, home and high-rise fire, flood, shelter-in-place
intro: What official guides say to do during and right after an earthquake, tsunami warning, hurricane, tornado or thunderstorm, wildfire or wildfire smoke, home or high-rise fire, flood, or chemical or radiation emergency, and how to plan an evacuation without a car — and how to get a go-bag and family plan ready beforehand.

limits.text: Do NOT get in a doorway during an earthquake — it doesn't protect from falling objects — and do not run outside.
If there are major cracks in the chimney or foundation, or the home or its utilities have shifted, get everyone out.
If you turned the gas off, do not turn it on again yourself; let the gas company inspect and restore it.
Do not use matches, lighters, candles, camp stoves or electrical equipment until you are sure there are no gas leaks.
If crawlspace walls have slid or are visibly leaning, turn off gas at the meter and do not reoccupy until a home safety evaluation.
Damaged or shifted rooftop solar panels are a falling or fire hazard; switch off the solar feed if possible and contact a qualified professional.
In a tsunami area, after a strong quake or a natural warning go to high ground or inland at once — do not wait for an official warning.
A tsunami is a series of waves that may continue for hours; the next wave may be larger. Return only when officials say it is safe.
If authorities tell you to evacuate for a wildfire, leave immediately; if trapped, call 9-1-1, but help could be delayed or impossible.
Authorities will never advise you to stay and fight an approaching wildfire.
Once out of a burning home, stay out; never go back inside for possessions, pets or people.
Do not walk, swim or drive through floodwater; just a foot of moving water can sweep a vehicle away. Do not climb into a closed attic.
Underground or downed power lines can electrically charge water; do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or you are standing in water.
When the calm eye of a hurricane passes over, the storm is not over; stay inside until emergency officials say it is safe.
Mobile and manufactured homes are unsafe in a tornado; choose a sturdier shelter before a watch or warning.
Do not try to outrun a tornado in a vehicle, and do not stop under a freeway, overpass or trees.
In a thunderstorm, avoid running water and landline phones; electricity can travel through plumbing and phone lines.
Young children and older adults should not use fire extinguishers; ask the fire department for training.
Outdoor areas, vehicles and mobile homes do NOT provide adequate shelter from nuclear fallout.
In a high-rise fire, use the stairs; do not use the elevator unless the fire department tells you to.
Never open a door that feels hot. If smoke, heat or flames block every exit, stay in the room with the door closed and call the fire department to say where you are.
